llm.reply:
KRAS encodes a small GTPase that functions as a molecular switch in downstream signaling pathways [11: "encodes a protein that is a member of the small GTPase superfamily"][26: "acts as a molecular switch to persistently stimulate downstream signaling pathways"]. A single activating amino-acid substitution produces a transforming protein implicated in lung adenocarcinoma, pancreatic ductal carcinoma, and colorectal carcinoma [11: "A single amino acid substitution is responsible for an activating mutation"].

## GTPase Signaling Function

The KRAS gene product belongs to the Kirsten ras oncogene homolog family within the small GTPase superfamily [11: "a Kirsten ras oncogene homolog from the mammalian ras gene family, encodes a protein that is a member of the small GTPase superfamily"]. Mutations in approximately 40% of colorectal cancer cases constitutively activate KRAS, persistently stimulating proliferation and survival signaling [26: "constitutive activation of the KRAS protein, which acts as a molecular switch to persistently stimulate downstream signaling pathways, including cell proliferation and survival"].

## Oncogenic Transformation

Oncogenic KRAS contributes to multiple cancer hallmarks, including suppression of antitumor immunity and promotion of angiogenesis and tumor invasion [28: "Oncogenic KRAS (KRAS*) contributes to many cancer hallmarks"][28: "KRAS* suppresses antitumor immunity to promote tumor invasion and metastasis"]. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, KRAS is mutated in up to 90% of cases, making it the most prevalent oncogenic driver in that disease [29: "The Kirsten ras sarcoma virus (KRAS) oncogene is mutated in up to 90% of all pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas"].

## Isoform Diversity

Alternative splicing of the KRAS transcript produces two isoforms that differ in the C-terminal region [11: "Alternative splicing leads to variants encoding two isoforms that differ in the C-terminal region"].

The KRAS gene product functions as a small GTPase, acting as a molecular switch that stimulates downstream signaling pathways including cell proliferation and survival [11: "member of the small GTPase superfamily"][26: "acts as a molecular switch to persistently stimulate downstream signaling pathways, including cell proliferation and survival"]. A single amino acid substitution can produce an activating mutation, and the resulting transforming protein is implicated in lung adenocarcinoma, pancreatic ductal carcinoma, and colorectal carcinoma [11: "A single amino acid substitution is responsible for an activating mutation"]. The gene is designated KRAS PROTOONCOGENE, GTPase [4], with the symbol KRAS [1] and the name KRAS [5].

## ClinVar Sequence Variants

The retrieved ClinVar records include NM_004985.5(KRAS):c.458ATG[1] (p.Asp154del) [3], NM_004985.5(KRAS):c.36T>C (p.Gly12=) [10], NM_004985.5(KRAS):c.337C>T (p.Leu113=) [15], NM_033360.4(KRAS):c.524A>G (p.Glu175Gly) [19], and NM_004985.5(KRAS):c.417T>A (p.Ile139=) [23]. The Gly12 variant is notable because glycine-12 substitutions are the most prevalent oncogenic KRAS alleles, with the G12C mutant now clinically targeted by covalent inhibitors such as sotorasib [27: "KRAS (G12C) inhibitors, such as AMG510 (sotorasib) and MRTX849 (adagrasib)"][30: "replacing glycine at position 12 with cysteine (G12C), which is clinically drugged through covalent inhibitors"].

## KRAS in Colorectal Cancer

KRAS is mutated in approximately 40% of colorectal cancer cases, and mutation testing is now routine clinical practice before treating metastatic disease [26: "mutations in approximately 40% of all CRC cases"][26: "KRAS mutation testing is a routine clinical practice before treating metastatic cases"]. Oncogenic KRAS transforms carcinoma-associated fibroblasts into lipid-rich CAFs that produce VEGFA, driving angiogenesis and disease progression [28: "KRAS* transforms the phenotype of carcinoma-associated fibroblasts (CAF) into lipid-laden CAFs, promoting angiogenesis and tumor progression"]. The entity name Kras appears in the literature [6], and key publications include PMID 34742312 [8], PMID 34776511 [13], PMID 37768068 [17], PMID 38686056 [21], and PMID 39298590 [25].

## Pan-KRAS Degraders and Pancreatic Targeting

A heterobifunctional small molecule degrades 13 of 17 prevalent oncogenic KRAS alleles, producing more sustained pathway suppression than inhibition alone [30: "potently degrades 13 out of 17 of the most prevalent oncogenic KRAS alleles"][30: "KRAS degradation results in more profound and sustained pathway modulation"]. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, KRAS is mutated in up to 90% of cases, with G12D, G12V, and G12R predominating and the G12D-directed inhibitor MRTX1133 entering clinical trials [29: "mutated in up to 90% of all pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas"][29: "KRAS G12D-directed MRTX1133 inhibitor has entered clinical trials"]. Retrieved trial names include Sorafenib in Combination With Irinotecan in Metastatic Colorectal Cancer Patients With KRAS Mutated Tumors [7], PREMIUM, Observational Study [12], A Trial of mFOLFIRI With MEK162 in Patients With Advanced RAS (HRAS, NRAS, or KRAS) Positive Metastatic Colorectal Cancers [16], Frequency of EGFR and KRAS Mutations and Clinical-prognostic Correlation in Brazilian Lung Cancer Patients [20], and A Phase 1/2, Study Evaluating the Safety, Tolerability, PK, and Efficacy of Sotorasib (AMG 510) in Subjects With Solid Tumors With a Specific KRAS Mutation (CodeBreaK 100) [24]. Additional retrieved PubMed titles are Role of oncogenic KRAS in the prognosis, diagnosis and treatment of colorectal cancer [2], KRAS mutation: from undruggable to druggable in cancer [9], Oncogenic KRAS Drives Lipofibrogenesis to Promote Angiogenesis and Colon Cancer Progression [14], Targeting KRAS in pancreatic cancer [18], and Targeting cancer with small-molecule pan-KRAS degraders [22].
